books.title: Storing for the Storm
books.subtitle: A good, hearty meal ready when you're overwhelmed
books.blurb: Prep ahead so you don't have to worry about it — a quick, good, hearty meal in the freezer or the pantry, ready for when you're overwhelmed.
books.intro:
This is a cookbook where I'm going to tie in psychology and the concept of stressful eating, and the things we can prep in advance so that we don't have to worry about it. We just have a quick, good, easy meal in the freezer or the pantry, ready to go. It's a collection of recipes, some for larger groups of people, some for a couple people, but all with the intention of making a really good, hearty meal that, when you're overwhelmed, is exactly what hits the spot.

The Green Goddess Goup is the first recipe in this one.
books.printTeaser: Want the full book? Green Goddess Goup is the first recipe from it.

recipes.title: Green Goddess Goup
recipes.quote: A lot of it is intuitive cooking, and I kinda wanna teach people to do intuitive cooking through this process... we're trained that we have to know the exact recipe. That's one of the biggest things to understand here.
recipes.summary: So I've done this dish many times, but I always forget to write stuff down. The Green Goddess Goup is the stock. This is not the full meal, this is the stock that you make that then you put the stuff in. It's very simplistic. These do not have to be exact. You can use whatever you want. This is just the portions I'm using while writing this recipe. It changes every single time.

yield.basis: this batch came out to 11 quarts exactly; it was exactly what I thought it would be

storage: A good one for the freezer and storage.

ingredients.prep: I may have used a little less
fresh or frozen; the one pound is often one bag

ingredients.item: any of your green stuff in the freezer

ingredients.prep: depending on how bitter you want it
a little handful, whatever you have on hand

steps.title: Load up the pot and bring it to a boil.
steps.text: You take a big pot of water, and I'm using about, let's say, 12 quarts of water in this pot. Put in your greens and whatever else green you have in the freezer you gotta get rid of. It's okay if it's a little freezer burn. Just dump it right in, put the moisture in there, don't worry about it. Cook it on high and bring it to a boil.

steps.title: Boil, then turn it down to a simmer.
steps.text: When it boils for about three to five minutes, turn it down to a simmer. If you let it boil too long, it's not going to hurt it. It will change the flavor slightly, it will bring it down a little bit so it's a deeper kind of flavor, and you don't want to over-salt it at that point, so if you forget about it, just know to be careful in the salt.

stove.electric: If you're on an electric stove, and I strongly dislike cooking on electric stoves, turn it down to about two to three, normally. Let it come down to a boil, and check it in about ten minutes, and double check if it's got a nice little simmer going. If not, crank it up a little bit.
stove.gas: If you're on a gas one, it means you already know how to cook with the stove. Just turn it down until you start seeing it calm down from a boil, down to a simmer, and hold it there. Normally it's maybe a little under medium at first, and it goes down to in between low and medium, so about a three or four. For those of you who are just learning to cook, this may matter. For someone who is cooking for a while, you probably kinda get what I mean, how every stove is a little bit different, but the gas one is much easier to adjust down to a simmer.

steps.title: Simmer about an hour, and watch the color.
steps.lookFor: the color dramatically changes to a darker green, not as bright green.
steps.text: You let that cook for about an hour. Around, say, 45 minutes-ish, you should see the color dramatically change to a darker green color, not as bright green. That's how you know the fibers are broken down. We don't wanna break down the fibers all the way to mush, that's why we don't overboil it, but you want it broken down enough that the immersion blender grabs it and purees it. Sometimes things are a little thicker, but you'll see it turn that color.

steps.title: Blend it.
steps.text: Take out your immersion blender, or if you're doing it in a blender on the counter, just dump it in carefully. Do not hurt yourself. Blend that all together.

steps.title: Season it, add the bay leaves and cilantro, and cook another 30 to 45 minutes.
steps.text: After we puree it, we add all those spices to it and the bay leaves, plus a little handful of cilantro with stems, whatever you have on hand, right on the top of it, and we let it cook another half hour to forty-five minutes. A little bit longer makes a little bit deeper flavor. The miso is optional. It adds a tang to it. I like it.

steps.title: Pull the bay leaves, add the coconut milk, and blend again.
steps.text: Take out the bay leaves. Add in two cans of coconut milk, puree that again, and let it cook for about another five to ten minutes. We can always add a little bit more water. This is about consistency.

steps.title: Cool it down and quart it out.
steps.text: Turn it off and let it cool until you're ready to quart it out.

parts.title: Part 2: Make it your stew
parts.lede: Here's what you can add to it to make your dish delicious, whenever you take it out of the freezer. Depending on how they're prepped, they need to get cooked and then added into it. If something requires longer cooking time, put it in there for longer. Most things coming out of a can, you can just dump them right in.

To finish: a squeeze of lime, chili crisp or hot sauce, a handful of cashews

subsections.title: Optional, for a little more meat to it

items.text: Ramen noodles, specifically ones that are not plastic. I'm being literal: don't eat the plastic ones, the ones with weird chemicals. Grab one like Lotus Ramen, that's a brown rice millet flour, that's a good one. There's other ones that are organic flour that aren't weird chemicals.

parts.closing: Pretty much, you can put almost anything you want in here. That's just a few. See what else tastes good. This is a stew that you get to make yourself. A bisque of the green goop.

notes.text: "Any of your green stuff in your freezer, throw it in there. It won't change the flavor that much, it'll probably make it taste better. But the whole point is, Green Goddess Goup, all that good green in there, let's get the green. But not other veggies outside of that." Broccoli stalks, or asparagus stalks you were saving for a cream of asparagus soup and forgot about.
Frozen veggies bring water from the ice on them, plus their own water content, so it won't cook down too much. It might be a little different when it's fresh.

The why: "The whole point of this is to get the GGG, the goop, through the system. You want it broken down. Sometimes you wanna have the food more fibrous, tougher, like the connective tissue when you're eating kale... good for the tougher parts of the body. This is to nourish the entire body, to keep it warm and full and cozy when you're camping, when you're a little cold, and just in general warm the heart. All those greens go to that core area to warm it."
